# HyperFrames

HyperFrames renders HTML to video by seeking a paused timeline frame by frame, so every render is identical; the person edits the same files in the Studio preview. Use it unless another framework or a plain browser recording is asked for. Run the CLI as `npx hyperframes <command>` (`/hyperframes-cli`); at the start of a new video, `npx hyperframes usage --json` reports the person's remaining plan usage (say "unknown" when it is).

`index.html` is the root composition: it declares the video's variables and mounts one scene per sub-composition from `compositions/`. Media and fonts live in `assets/`. A new project: `npx hyperframes init <dir>`. A website as the subject: `npx hyperframes capture <url> --json`.

Build what was asked: no voiceover or captions and no new aspect ratio unless the request or the source calls for them; a film over ~15 s that tells something gets music and sound on its visible actions unless the person asked for silence (`references/sound.md`). Before hand-writing a named effect, transition, caption style, chart or card, search the registry (`/hyperframes-registry`). Any media (a presenter or avatar, footage, voice, music): `/media-use`, which says when HeyGen is needed and what is free. `npx hyperframes check --json` reports most violations with a `Fix:` line.

1. Every timed element has `class="clip"`, `data-start` and `data-duration` in seconds, and shows over `[start, start + duration)`: land an end state just before its end. `data-track-index` is only a Studio lane; paint order is `z-index`.
2. The video's length is the root's `data-duration`: overrun is cut, an early end holds the last frame.
3. Each composition builds one paused timeline and registers it after its tweens: `window.__timelines["<data-composition-id>"] = tl`.
4. No `Date.now()`, unseeded `Math.random()`, network fetches, timers or `repeat: -1`. Everything visible is a function of timeline time.
5. Never tween `display`, `visibility` or `autoAlpha` on a `.clip`; animate a child.
6. No CSS `transform` on an element GSAP transforms; animate transforms, not `left`/`top`/`width`/`height`.
7. Never `play()`, `pause()` or seek media. A `<video>` keeps its sound with `data-has-audio="true"`, else it is `muted`; music, voice, replacement sound and J/L cuts are a separate `<audio>`.

10. Asset paths are root-relative (`assets/...`), in sub-compositions too.
11. Grades, grain, blur and vignettes on footage go through `npx hyperframes media-treatment` (`/media-use`), never CSS filters.
12. A scene file puts its styles, markup and scripts inside `<template>` and styles its root as `#root`. Intended overflow or overlap: `data-layout-allow-overflow`, `data-layout-allow-overlap`.

- Copy, brand colours and swappable media are variables (`data-var-text`, `data-var-src`, `var(--id)`).

# 3D, simulations and generative pieces

Use 3D when the film earns it: an object or a set as the payoff, a product, a simulation that explains. Loading Three.js, WebGPU, p5 or canvas and the seek protocol are in `../runtimes.md`.

## Deterministic by construction

- Draw every frame from timeline time in the `hf-seek` listener; frames render out of order.
- Simulate once at load (physics, agents, particles) into arrays, then look up the state at `t`: `render(t)` stays a pure function. Heavy setup (meshes, shader compiles, the simulation) registers a `window.__hf.buildReady` promise.
- Seed every random choice; a seeded hash of the index, never `Math.random()`.

## Camera and story

- One hero object beats a crowd. Fly through or into it rather than orbiting it: one dive is worth ten turns.
- Cutaways, exploded views and chapters with one caption line each, plus labels with real numbers, turn a simulation into an explanation instead of eye candy.
- Product UI is never tilted into 3D; only generated content tilts.

## Light and materials

- Light it with a warm key, a cool rim and a dark environment with two or three soft strips; turn the environment, not the object, so highlights sweep across it; a contact shadow under the object.
- Bloom eats detail: keep it to the brightest points. Glossy metal under a low light gives white streaks: roughness about 0.45 or more, environment intensity about 0.5.
- One NaN pixel turns a whole frame black through bloom: clamp values that can divide by zero.

## Check it

Snapshot the dive and the payoff (`../review.md`); a frame that takes too long to draw slows every render, so profile the heaviest moment once.
# Characters, mascots and story shorts

A character gives every transition a cause and gives the film its jokes: it carries the result into the player, rejects its own first try, reads the manual. After Effects characters come in through Lottie (`../runtimes.md`).

## Acting

- Mood changes go through a take: anticipation, a squash, the new face, a settle. A face never snaps from one state to the next.
- Squash and stretch, anticipation, overshoot and follow-through belong to the character. Here an idle breath or blink is life, not a tell; the tells about breathing and bounce in `../motion.md` are about titles and UI.
- Code moves every part at once, on one curve, by the same amount. Offset the parts (head leads, arms follow), vary the amounts, and never move both arms, both eyes or a crowd in unison.
- Contact sells it: feet on the ground, props held by the hand, eyes on what they look at.

## Reads

Each action is one read. Lead the eye to where it will happen, play the action fast, and let its meaning land slowly: hold the reaction. A sign or caption that repeats what the action already shows is the classic failure.

## Build

- A rig is a set of parameters over time: position, squash, arm angles, an eye state and a mouth state per moment. Write mood changes as keyed states (`[[t0,"normal"],[t1,"scared"]]`) the rig eases between.
- Hand-drawn life: redraw the outlines about 12 times a second with a jitter seeded by `Math.floor(t * 12)`, so the line boils while the character holds still, and every render matches.
- A long piece is one chapter per sub-composition, all drawing from the same rig and helpers.
# Animation runtimes

HyperFrames seeks each frame on its own, so motion must be a function of time, never of the previous frame. Full GSAP reference: `npx hyperframes docs gsap`.

## GSAP facts that bite

- Register the timeline last. Building inside `document.fonts.ready.then(…)` or another async callback is fine if you register at the end of it; registering first renders blank (`gsap_timeline_registered_before_async_build`).
- Place tweens at absolute seconds (`tl.to(el, {…}, 2.4)`). Set start states in the tween (`fromTo`), not in CSS.
- Measure layout once before building tweens, never inside `onUpdate`.
- Finite repeats only: `repeat: Math.max(0, Math.floor(duration / cycle) - 1)`.
- Seed randomness with a small PRNG (mulberry32).
- A scene's timeline can't reach elements outside its file, and two timelines must not animate the same property of one element.
- Transforms on a `<span>` need `display: inline-block` or `block`.
- Text that must fit a width: `window.__hyperframes.fitTextFontSize(text, { fontFamily, fontWeight, maxWidth })` returns `{ fontSize }`; `window.__hyperframes.pretext` measures text without a reflow.

## Other runtimes

| Runtime                      | Use for                           | How HyperFrames drives it                                                                        |
| ---------------------------- | --------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| CSS `@keyframes`             | Simple loops and decoration       | Found automatically; finite iterations, `animation-fill-mode: both`, `data-start` on the element |
| WAAPI                        | Native keyframes                  | `element.animate(…, { fill: "both" })` then `pause()`; times are document time, so use `delay`   |
| Lottie / dotLottie           | After Effects exports, characters | `autoplay: false`, always set `loop`, push the instance to `window.__hfLottie`                   |
| anime.js v4                  | Existing anime code               | `autoplay: false`, push to `window.__hfAnime`, `anime.createSeededRandom`                        |
| Three.js, WebGPU, p5, canvas | 3D and generative                 | Draw from `e.detail.time` in an `hf-seek` listener; set `data-duration` on the root              |

# preview, play, render, publish

Serve, render, and share commands.

## preview

```bash
npx hyperframes preview                   # foreground on a TTY; persistent in agent shells
npx hyperframes preview --background      # explicit persistent session
npx hyperframes preview --foreground --json # ready JSON, then remain attached
npx hyperframes preview --background --port 4567 # agent-safe custom port (default 3002)
npx hyperframes preview --selection --json # print the current Studio selection and exit
npx hyperframes preview --context --json  # print compact agent context from Studio
```

Hot-reloads on file changes. Opens Studio in the browser automatically — the full timeline editor, where the user can play the video and edit anything by hand before rendering. This is the review surface, not just a viewer.

When handing a project back to the user, use the Studio project URL, not the source `index.html` path:

```text
http://localhost:<port>/#project/<project-name>
```

Use the actual port and project directory name; treat `index.html` as source-code context, not the preview surface. For example, after `npx hyperframes preview --background --port 3017` in `codex-openai-video`, report `http://localhost:3017/#project/codex-openai-video`.

Two ways a handed URL turns out dead — check both before handing it back: the URL is missing its `#project/<project-name>` hash (Studio loads but has no project to open), or the server is not actually running. Bare `preview` automatically creates a managed persistent session in a non-TTY agent shell; `--background` remains the clearest explicit form. Verify the printed URL returns HTTP 200, keep it alive for the whole review, and stop it explicitly with `npx hyperframes preview --stop` afterward. Use the printed URL as-is: HyperFrames URL-encodes project names that contain route metacharacters.

### Agent context from Studio selection

`preview --context` and `preview --selection` are the agent bridge into a running Studio session. They do **not** start a new server; they find the active preview server for the current project, read agent-useful state from Studio, print it, and exit.

Use it when the user gives deictic edit instructions like "change this", "move the selected element", "make the card I clicked bigger", or "fix the current selection":

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection
```

The compact context payload includes the selected element's source file, composition path, current timeline time, `data-hf-id` / selector target, bounding box, text content, and a thumbnail URL for the selected element. Prefer `selection.target.hfId` when present; fall back to `selection.target.selector` only when no stable `data-hf-id` exists. If `selection` is `null`, inspect `errors.selection.code` (for example, `no-selection`).

Keep agent context small by asking only for the slices you need:

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields lint
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection,lint
```

Use `--context-detail full` only when the edit genuinely needs heavy selection fields such as `computedStyles`, `inlineStyles`, `dataAttributes`, or editable text-field metadata:

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection --context-detail full
```

`preview --selection --json` remains available when you explicitly want the full selected-element payload and do not need lint/server context.

Failure modes:

| Code                       | Meaning                                                                    |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `preview-not-running`      | Start Studio first with `npx hyperframes preview --background`.            |
| `ambiguous-preview-server` | Multiple matching Studio servers are open; rerun with one listed `--port`. |
| `preview-port-mismatch`    | The requested `--port` is not one of the matching Studio servers.          |
| `no-selection`             | Studio is open, but the user has not selected an element yet.              |
| `selection-unavailable`    | The running preview server does not expose selection context cleanly.      |

If there is no selection, ask the user to click the target element in Studio and rerun the command. If the server error lists candidate ports, rerun the same command with `--port <candidate>`. Do not infer the target from a screenshot when the CLI can give a stable element target.

## play (lightweight player)

```bash
npx hyperframes play                  # current project, port 3003
npx hyperframes play ./my-video       # specific project
npx hyperframes play --port 8080      # custom port
```

`play` serves the composition through the embeddable `<hyperframes-player>` web component instead of the full Studio UI. Use it when sharing a preview link or when Studio is heavier than needed (no editor, no panels). `play` reports the plain `http://localhost:<port>` URL — no `#project/<name>` fragment (that's a Studio routing convention only `preview` uses).

The player's `playback-rate` attribute (preview speed control, drives the timeline's `timeScale`) is clamped to `[0.1, 5]`; values `≤ 0` or non-finite fall back to `1`. This is a preview/playback knob, not a composition `data-*` attribute — authored motion still renders at `1×`.

### Launching with an external browser (preview + play)

Both `preview` and `play` can open inside an explicit Chromium-compatible browser instead of the OS default. Two use cases: isolated Chromium profile, or external CDP attach (DevTools / Playwright / Puppeteer / browser-MCP). **HyperFrames itself does not own CDP automation** — this only exposes the endpoint; whatever connects to it is your problem. Not to be confused with `--browser-gpu` (a `render` flag controlling Chrome GPU access during capture).

When handing a project back to the user, use the Studio project URL, not the source `index.html` path:

```text
http://localhost:<port>/#project/<project-name>
```

Use the actual port and project directory name; treat `index.html` as source-code context, not the preview surface. For example, after `npx hyperframes preview --background --port 3017` in `codex-openai-video`, report `http://localhost:3017/#project/codex-openai-video`.

Two ways a handed URL turns out dead — check both before handing it back: the URL is missing its `#project/<project-name>` hash (Studio loads but has no project to open), or the server is not actually running. Bare `preview` automatically creates a managed persistent session in a non-TTY agent shell; `--background` remains the clearest explicit form. Verify the printed URL returns HTTP 200, keep it alive for the whole review, and stop it explicitly with `npx hyperframes preview --stop` afterward. Use the printed URL as-is: HyperFrames URL-encodes project names that contain route metacharacters.

### Agent context from Studio selection

`preview --context` and `preview --selection` are the agent bridge into a running Studio session. They do **not** start a new server; they find the active preview server for the current project, read agent-useful state from Studio, print it, and exit.

Use it when the user gives deictic edit instructions like "change this", "move the selected element", "make the card I clicked bigger", or "fix the current selection":

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection
```

The compact context payload includes the selected element's source file, composition path, current timeline time, `data-hf-id` / selector target, bounding box, text content, and a thumbnail URL for the selected element. Prefer `selection.target.hfId` when present; fall back to `selection.target.selector` only when no stable `data-hf-id` exists. If `selection` is `null`, inspect `errors.selection.code` (for example, `no-selection`).

Keep agent context small by asking only for the slices you need:

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields lint
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection,lint
```

Use `--context-detail full` only when the edit genuinely needs heavy selection fields such as `computedStyles`, `inlineStyles`, `dataAttributes`, or editable text-field metadata:

```bash
npx hyperframes preview --context --json --context-fields selection --context-detail full
```

| Code                       | Meaning                                                                    |
| -------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `preview-not-running`      | Start Studio first with `npx hyperframes preview --background`.            |
| `ambiguous-preview-server` | Multiple matching Studio servers are open; rerun with one listed `--port`. |
| `preview-port-mismatch`    | The requested `--port` is not one of the matching Studio servers.          |
| `no-selection`             | Studio is open, but the user has not selected an element yet.              |
| `selection-unavailable`    | The running preview server does not expose selection context cleanly.      |

If there is no selection, ask the user to click the target element in Studio and rerun the command. If the server error lists candidate ports, rerun the same command with `--port <candidate>`. Do not infer the target from a screenshot when the CLI can give a stable element target.

## play (lightweight player)

```bash
npx hyperframes play                  # current project, port 3003
npx hyperframes play ./my-video       # specific project
npx hyperframes play --port 8080      # custom port
```

`play` serves the composition through the embeddable `<hyperframes-player>` web component instead of the full Studio UI. Use it when sharing a preview link or when Studio is heavier than needed (no editor, no panels). `play` reports the plain `http://localhost:<port>` URL — no `#project/<name>` fragment (that's a Studio routing convention only `preview` uses).

The player's `playback-rate` attribute (preview speed control, drives the timeline's `timeScale`) is clamped to `[0.1, 5]`; values `≤ 0` or non-finite fall back to `1`. This is a preview/playback knob, not a composition `data-*` attribute — authored motion still renders at `1×`.

Both `preview` and `play` can open inside an explicit Chromium-compatible browser instead of the OS default. Two use cases: isolated Chromium profile, or external CDP attach (DevTools / Playwright / Puppeteer / browser-MCP). **HyperFrames itself does not own CDP automation** — this only exposes the endpoint; whatever connects to it is your problem. # Review

You wrote the timeline, so you know what happens; the viewer sees it once, at full speed, often on a phone. Review is how you see the film as they will: as a harsh motion director, not a proud author. `check` catches what is broken; this pass catches what is weak. Run it after `check` passes, on every new film and on any edit that changes timing or layout, before you reply or render.

## 1. Measure, then look

1. `npx hyperframes check --json`. Besides errors it warns on craft it can measure: a line on screen too briefly to read (`line_unread`), more than 3 s with nothing changing (`dead_stretch`), text under 2.6% of the frame's short side (`text_below_floor`), an empty first frame (`first_frame_empty`, the thumbnail on social players), a film over 15 s with no sound (`film_silent`). A warning is a question, not a rule: fix it, or keep it on purpose and say why in the note (a deliberate hold carries `data-hold`).
2. `npx hyperframes snapshot --review` writes three sheets: each scene just after it starts and at its middle, plus each `data-beat`, a strip across every cut (−0.2 s to +0.2 s), and the beat frames at phone width (360 px). Open all three.
3. Motion between the beats: `snapshot --range START,END --frames 8` around the hero move and the payoff; `keyframes --shot` for a path that must arc or land.
4. The rendered file: `npx hyperframes audio <video> --json` shows whether sound is there, where it hits and how loud it is. You cannot hear it; say so.

Trust the numbers over your eye where they disagree: a clipped label or a 0.6 s line looks fine on a contact sheet.

## 2. What to look for

First, describe each beat frame in one sentence as a stranger would, naming every object; an object you would have to explain ("those bars are mirrors") is a P0. Then read the beat frames in order: do they tell a story a stranger follows, each one causing the next? Compare each with its shot in `SPEC.md`; what does not match is a note. Then name every default the frames show (`spec.md` "BANNED by default", or one not on the list yet), add each to the BANNED line, and fix them before anything else.

Then go through the sheets once per question:

| Question                      | What it catches                                                                                                                                    |
| ----------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Does it read as what it is?   | A shape that reads as another object, a material that reads as plastic, a product screen that reads as a mockup, a face or mascot that reads wrong |
| Does the subject separate?    | Subject and ground too close in value, two focal points in one frame, the eye with nowhere to go                                                   |
| Framing and contact           | Crops, text at the edge or under platform UI, collisions at a seam, things floating that should touch                                              |
| Timing as a first-time viewer | A read shorter than its words (`story.md` §6), something that pops on with no move, a jump at a cut, everything moving at once on one curve        |
| Tells                         | Which items of `story.md` §8 and `motion.md` "Defaults that look generated" are on screen                                                          |
| The pictures alone            | With the words covered, do the beat frames still tell the storyline?                                                                               |
| The phone sheet               | Can every line meant to be read be read at 360 px?                                                                                                 |

## 3. Notes and fixes

Write each problem as one line: `t=4.2s · where · problem → exact change · what stays`. Rank them:

- **P0** breaks the read or the contract: unreadable, wrong, broken, a tell in the hero shot.
- **P1** weakens the film: a dead stretch, a soft payoff, a seam that jumps.
- **P2** polish.

Fix every P0 and the P1s worth their time: text first, then timing, then detail. Then snapshot only what you changed, once. A second pass only when a P0 is still open. Never score the film out of 10: a score finds nothing to fix. When a fix does not hold, snapshot the frames on either side of the problem, list every difference, and change only the line that causes it. A film that feels busy: remove a third of the motion and keep the moves that lead the eye.

A fresh pair of eyes, when your host can start a sub-agent: give it only `STORYBOARD.md` and the three sheets, ask for P0 and P1 lines in the format above, and keep editing to yourself. Commit or copy the project before you fix, so a fix that makes things worse can be rolled back.

## 4. The delivery note

Write `REVIEW.md` at the project root and put its short form in your reply:

- the creative calls you made, and the storylines you did not build;
- what you measured and what you only looked at; what nobody checked (the sound was measured, not heard);
- the weakest shot, and what you would change with more time;
- warnings you kept on purpose, and why.

The next turn reads it before changing anything.

3:Use `lint` for fast static feedback while iterating. Use `check` as the required final gate: it reruns the same linter, then audits runtime, layout, motion, and contrast in one browser session. Do not chain a redundant standalone `lint` immediately before `check`. `snapshot` is the standalone utility for capturing still frames and zoomed crops. `validate`, `inspect`, and `layout` still run but are deprecated: `check` covers all of them in one invocation.
5:## Discipline (motion-heavy work)
13:- State motion intent in a `*.motion.json` sidecar so `check` verifies it automatically (entrances firing under seek, stagger order, in-frame, liveness). This is the closest automated proxy for "watch the MP4" and catches render-vs-preview bugs the eye misses (see **Motion verification** below).
33:npx hyperframes check --json             # agent-readable envelope {ok, browserSkipped, lint, runtime, layout, motion, contrast, craft, hdr, snapshots}
44:One command, one Chrome boot. `check` runs the linter first and skips the browser entirely when lint reports errors. When the browser never ran (lint errors, a linter crash, or a browser launch failure), `browserSkipped` is `true` and the `layout`, `motion` and `contrast` sections are empty, not clean. Otherwise it loads the bundled composition once, wires runtime listeners before navigation, and sweeps one seek grid running every audit per sample:
47:- **Layout**: text extending outside its container or the canvas, text clipped by its own box, held text overlaps and occlusion (with an approximate covered fraction), children escaping clipping containers. Text under a transparent `<video>` (a `remove-background` cutout) is measured per word against the frame's alpha: partial cover is info with the share hidden, a word 80% hidden or two neighbouring words each half hidden is an error, and a frame that cannot be read falls back to opaque with a `video_alpha_unread` note.
48:- **Motion**: `*.motion.json` sidecar assertions against the same seeked timeline (see below).
52:  - `dead_stretch`: more than 3 s where the `keepsMoving` classifier sees nothing change. The final 3 s and any time a `data-hold` element is on screen are exempt; it stays quiet when `sweep_static` fires or a whole-composition `keepsMoving` assertion sets the limit.
54:  - `first_frame_empty`: frame 0 paints nothing but the background (no text, image, video, canvas or svg); it is the thumbnail on social players.
59:**Severity is persistence-aware.** A dynamic issue observed at a single grid sample (an entrance/exit transient) demotes to info and never gates. Issues held across samples gate the exit code, a held `content_overlap` is an error, and a held, partially-visible `canvas_overflow` breaching ≥5% of the canvas promotes to warning. Coordinate-frame findings (`escaped_container`, `panel_out_of_canvas`, `connector_detached`) flag geometry computed in one frame but rendered in another — an element far outside its offset parent, a painted panel stuck across the canvas edge, a connector line detached from every node. Text drawn into a `<canvas>` has no DOM box, so `canvas_overflow` cannot see it; `canvas_content_at_edge` warns when a canvas's pixels show sharp content (drawn text, hard shapes) along the frame edge — mark intentional full-bleed art (particles, photos) with `data-layout-allow-overflow`. If a 3s+ composition shows no visible change across every sample, `check` fails with `sweep_static`: a frame that never changes while a GSAP timeline or tween, or a CSS or Web animation, holds the same time without ever finishing means the seek is not driving the page, so it refuses to pass. Any other frame that never changes (a still title card, an audio-only advance) is a warning that `--strict` fails; a composition meant to be still can take `data-no-timeline` on its root to skip it. The fingerprint includes per-element opacity, so opacity-only reveals (code typing, staggered fades) count as motion — but only while they're still in flight at the sampled times. The classic trap is a reveal that completes early and then holds a static frame for the rest of the duration: every sample lands on the settled state and check warns that nothing on screen moved (`--strict` fails it). Spread the reveal across the timeline or give the hold a real next action (the cursor heading to the next control, the camera's next move); don't bolt on a slow drift, a blinking caret or a loop just to appease the check.
68:- `data-hold` — deliberate stillness: while this element is on screen, `dead_stretch` does not count the time.
74:npx hyperframes check --frame-check     # media (img/svg/video/canvas) out-of-frame detection
77:`--caption-zone` takes fractional band geometry (`x0/y0/x1/y1` required, 0-1 fractions of the composition's own canvas, portrait included) with optional `severity` and comma-separated `seek` fractions; it flags a text element's DOM box (`getBoundingClientRect`) that overlaps the band. Waive intentional lower-third copy with `data-layout-allow-caption-zone` on the element or its nearest wrapper (see Escape hatches). `--frame-check` reports media elements breaching the canvas beyond `max(120px, 6% of the min canvas dimension)`.
81:## Motion verification (`*.motion.json` sidecar)
83:`check` verifies **motion intent** against the same seeked timeline the renderer uses — the closest automated proxy for "render the MP4 and watch it". It catches render-vs-preview bugs layout sampling can't: an entrance reveal the seek lands past, a broken stagger order, an element drifting off-frame mid-tween, a frozen shot.
